title: Mini-Project 01 - What We Watched: Exploring Netflix Viewing Data
text:
Final Insights and Deliverable
Dear Netflix
My name is Jonathan Chan, a Data Analyst from Weylandt Consulting and Analytics. I’ve analyzed your data, seven of Netflix’s “What We Watched” reports, covering 511.6B hours of viewing from the first half of 2023 to the first half of 2026. Five patterns stood out to me, and I think each should shape how we spend in 2027
1. Invest in a few big hits, but keep a deep catalogue
Viewing is pretty uneven across titles on your platform. To measure this, I used the Gini coefficient, which economists use to measure inequality. It runs from 0%, where every title gets the same amount of viewing, to 100%, where one title gets all of it. Among TV titles, the score moved from 73.7% in 2023H2 to 75.5% in 2026H1, so viewing has become slightly more concentrated in the biggest shows (think of ONE PIECE or King The Land or Bridgerton). Adjusted for runtime, the 2026H1 score is 70.9%. In 2026H1:

The top 1% of titles captured 22.2% of watch time.
The ten biggest titles accounted for only 6.7%.
Titles outside the top 100 still made up 75.5% of viewing.

The big franchises are worth it: Stranger Things (keep milking it!) alone has generated 5.5B hours. I’d recommend putting our largest budgets behind a few potential franchises while keeping a consistent flow of mid-budget titles between major releases.
2. Make new Originals available worldwide
In 2026H1, titles available in every country made up 38.2% of the TV catalog but captured 49.1% of TV watch time. Across all periods, the average worldwide title drew 2.0 times the hours of one licensed only in certain regions. I recommend securing worldwide rights for every original at greenlight and using regional licensing only to fill market-specific gaps (there may be a slight bias from Dragon Ball Super Beerus being in Netflix JP and not global).
3. Keep TV series at the center
Movies are great and all, but in 2023H1, the only report in our data that includes both TV and film, series accounted for 70.6% of watch time, compared with 29.4% for films, specials, and unclassified titles. The most-watched title was The Night Agent: Season 1, generating 812.1M hours.
Long-running series are also our most dependable titles. Pablo Escobar, el patron del mal: Season 1 appeared in every report and never dropped below 105.5M hours in any six-month period.
For 2027, I’d prioritize serialized originals and renewals with strong baselines, using films to hold interest between seasons. Views aren’t profit, though, so production costs and subscriber retention should weigh in too.
4. Plan around the launch rush
Most viewing happens soon after release. I followed 238 titles released in the final month of a reporting period into the next report. Their launch window (only the days between release and the period’s end, a median of 19 days) captured a median of 60.0% of their combined viewing across both reports, versus 9.4% if viewing were spread evenly. Per day, the launch window ran 16.9 times higher than the following six months.
I recommend concentrating marketing around release dates. Whether nearby premieres steal viewers from each other is worth testing next.
5. Use live events selectively
Live programming went from 0.3% of watch time in 2024H2 to 0.5% in 2026H1, still a very small share of viewing.

The average live event drew 1.5M views, compared with 1.3M for the average pre-recorded TV title.
The biggest pre-recorded titles far outdrew the biggest live events: the top ten averaged 101.7M views, compared with 11.3M for the top ten live events.

I recommend a small number of high-profile live events, valued for attracting subscribers and advertisers rather than for replacing scripted hits. From what I’ve seen personally, the younger end of Gen Z loves live events with stakes.
Limitations

After 2023H1, our data includes only Netflix’s TV sheet, so film comparisons rely on 2023H1 alone and trends over time describe TV viewing.
Only titles with English-character names are included.
Netflix rounds hours to the nearest 100,000 and leaves out very small titles.
Views are estimated by dividing hours watched by runtime.
My split between series and films is based on a rule of thumb.

Even so, I don’t expect these gaps to change the overall conclusions, because the main patterns hold within every period that can be fairly compared.







NoteAI Usage Statement





AI disclosure, I used ChatGPT to help format the css for this project to get Netflix themed fonts and colors. I also used Claude for the Gini coefficient math but i drew the conclusion from it myself. After my first run through, I asked Claude to compare my work to the rubric and so I had it make the variables for me after i realized i shouldn’t hard code the numbers in my comparative analyses, so i can plug the variable into the memo I’d write myself.

# Calculate the Gini coefficient
gini <- function(x) {
  x <- sort(x[!is.na(x)])

  n <- length(x)

  if (n == 0 || sum(x) == 0) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }

  2 * sum(seq_len(n) * x) / (n * sum(x)) -
    (n + 1) / n
}

# Pounds of CO2 per unit, from EIA "Carbon Dioxide Emissions Coefficients"
# (released Sept 2024). Tailpipe accounting: bio-diesel blends (mostly B5-B20)
# and renewable diesel are counted at the diesel rate, i.e., we count all
# carbon that leaves the tailpipe. A sensitivity check further down gives
# renewable diesel a biogenic (zero) rate instead.
LB_CO2 <- c(
  diesel = 22.45, # Diesel and home heating fuel (distillate)
  gasoline = 18.73, # Finished motor gasoline (E10, as sold at the pump)
  lpg = 12.68, # Propane
  kerosene = 21.78,
  residual = 24.78, # Residual fuel oil (closest match to bunker fuel)
  # NTD reports CNG in gasoline-gallon equivalents (GGE): reported CNG bus
  # fuel economy (~2.5-4 mpg) is only plausible on an equivalent basis.
  # lbs per GGE = natural gas lbs/MMBtu x gasoline MMBtu/gallon.
  cng = 116.65 * (18.73 / 155.77),
  lng = 116.65 * 0.0848, # natural gas lbs/MMBtu x LNG MMBtu/gallon (BTS)
  ethanol = 18.73, # negligible volume; counted as finished gasoline

  geom_vline(xintercept = car_real_lb_per_mile, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text",
    x = car_lb_per_mile, y = label_y, hjust = -0.03, size = 3.6,
    label = paste0("Solo driver, CAFE car (", CAFE_MPG, " mpg)")
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = car_real_lb_per_mile, y = label_y + 0.6, hjust = -0.03, size = 3.6,
    label = paste0("Solo driver, real-world new car (", REAL_WORLD_MPG, " mpg)")
  ) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 1.9))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = CAR_COMPARISON_COLORS, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(
    title = "CO2 per passenger-mile by transit mode, 2025",
    subtitle = "National totals, compared with one person driving a CAFE-standard car",
    x = "Pounds of CO2 per passenger-mile", y = NULL,
    caption = paste0(
      "Sources: FTA National Transit Database (2025 Energy Consumption, ",
      "Service by Agency); EIA State Electricity Profiles and CO2 ",
      "coefficients;\nNHTSA CAFE standards (MY2026); EPA Automotive Trends ",
      "Report (MY2024 real-world fuel economy). Modes reported by fewer than ",
      "3 agencies omitted."
    )
  ) +
  theme_gta()









Emissions by Transit Mode: The National Picture
Before getting into the specific awards, we should look at how different transit modes are actually performing nationally. In 2025, US public transit generated about 8.9M metric tons of CO2 (That’s around 1.5 million adult African elephants, damn). Just a quick heads up that this excludes 6 transit records from PR since the EIA doesn’t have grid profiles for them.
But to be honest, judging transit just by total carbon output completely misses the point (as bad as the elephant example sounds). The whole goal of public transit is moving people efficiently. When we normalize this by ridership, the national average carbon footprint for public transit is 0.48 lbs of CO2 per passenger-mile.
For some context, a solo driver in the real world produces about 0.69 lbs of CO2 per mile. So yeah, taking transit is definitely a win compared to driving an average car. That said, transit as a whole still lags a bit behind the theoretical efficiency of a brand new CAFE standard car at 0.38 lbs of CO2 per mile. But unfortunately, nobody actually drives in perfect lab conditions.
When we break the data down by specific modes, a pretty clear hierarchy emerges:

The Most Efficient: Heavy Rail (subways) and Vanpools (a larger carpool like a van or SUV; discovered this term for the first time) are basically carrying the team, sitting at 0.19 and 0.19 lbs of CO2 per passenger-mile respectively. Even though they are on complete opposite ends of the infrastructure spectrum, both modes maximize their passenger density relative to the energy they consume which is very economically appreciated
The Middle Ground: Traditional bus systems average 0.75 lbs per passenger-mile, which puts them slightly above a real-world solo driver. This may feel bad, but it really just reflects how driving heavy diesel vehicles on routes that have low ridership during off-peak hours will reflect.
The Least Efficient: Demand Response (paratransit) and Ferries are the most carbon intensive modes. They generate 2.14 and 2.16 lbs of CO2 per passenger-mile respectively. We can give Demand Response a pass since it is a vital accessibility service that naturally operates with low passenger density and lives are literally on the line most of the time. Ferries on the other hand are just burning ungodly amounts of energy to push heavy boats across the water (but hey ferries are a vibe sometimes).

FIXED_ROUTE_MODES <- c(

MIN_UPT <- 100000

# Usage is summed only over modes that also report energy, so numerator and
# denominator always describe the same service. Agency-modes the NTD flags
# as a "questionable record" are dropped from both sides. Dropping the whole
# agency instead would remove, e.g., MTA NYC Transit over one flagged mode.
n_flagged_modes <- sum(EMISSIONS$flagged)
flagged_upt_share <- sum(EMISSIONS$upt[EMISSIONS$flagged]) / sum(EMISSIONS$upt)

AGENCY <- EMISSIONS |>
  filter(pmt > 0, upt > 0, !flagged) |>
  group_by(`NTD ID`) |>
  summarize(
    agency = first(agency),
    state = first(state),
    uza_name = first(uza_name),
    fixed_route = any(Mode %in% FIXED_ROUTE_MODES),
    modes = str_flatten_comma(sort(unique(Mode))),
    co2 = sum(co2_total),
    co2_renewable = sum(co2_renewable),
    co2_electric = sum(co2_electric),
    upt = sum(upt),
    pmt = sum(pmt),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    lb_per_pmt = co2 / pmt,
    lb_per_upt = co2 / upt,
    # biogenic sensitivity: renewable diesel counted as zero
    lb_per_pmt_biogenic = (co2 - co2_renewable) / pmt,

Methodology: Normalizing to Transit Usage
To evaluate environmental impact fairly, we normalized raw emissions against transit usage. We chose pounds of CO2 per passenger-mile as our primary metric rather than emissions per trip to be ‘fairer’. As the data shows, evaluating by trip heavily favors short-distance urban services like streetcars, while passenger-miles better capture the true distance-based environmental benefit of long-distance commuter buses compared to driving. We also restricted eligibility to fixed-route services. While demand-response systems are essential for community accessibility, their inherently low passenger density skews direct efficiency comparisons.
Because transit systems operate on vastly different scales (so we don’t compare the MTA and the Skyline from Honolulu), we grouped eligible agencies into three size classes based on annual trips: 159 Small (under 1M), 213 Medium (1M-20M), and 38 Large (over 20M). For quality control, we had to drop 99 agency records as they were flagged as questionable by the NTD, which accounted for 7% of total trips. Ultimately, out of 495 agencies with energy data, 420 operated fixed routes, leaving a final eligible pool of 410 agencies that met our 100K annual trip minimum.
Compared to a theoretical CAFE standard car, 94% of transit agencies are dirtier than driving solo, and 80% fall short of a real-world solo driver. However, because the absolute cleanest agencies (like major city subways) carry the vast majority of commuters, 45% of all transit passenger-miles are ridden on systems cleaner than a CAFE standard car, and 78% beat a real world car. Most transit agencies struggle with efficiency (for example, how common buses drive an empty bus at like 3am. It’s nice to have the security of knowing they’re always running for someone out there), but most transit riders use highly efficient systems.

Press Release (Task 8)

Greenest Transit Agency






Seattle Center Monorail. Photo: Cliff from Arlington, Virginia, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons







Adirondack Trailways. Photo: Secondarywaltz, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons





The Greenest Transit Agency award goes to systems with the lowest total carbon footprint per passenger-mile. In the Large category, SF BART in California won with 0.16 lbs CO2 per passenger-mile. This is 4.2 times better than the median large agency average of 0.67 lbs. In the Medium category, the Seattle Center Monorail in Washington won with 0.06 lbs CO2 per passenger-mile, beating the median by 15.8 times. In the Small category, Adirondack Trailways in New York won with 0.15 lbs CO2 per passenger-mile compared to a median of 1.40. These results are highly robust. The winners stay exactly the same in two of the three size classes even if we count renewable diesel as zero carbon.


Show All Code
winners_plot <- greenest |>
  mutate(label = paste0(agency, "\n", fmt_2(lb_per_pmt), " lbs"))

set.seed(9750) # reproducible jitter
ELIGIBLE |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lb_per_pmt, y = size)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = vs_car(lb_per_pmt, car_lb_per_mile)),
    height = 0.18, width = 0, alpha = 0.6, size = 2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = CAR_COMPARISON_COLORS, name = "Each dot is one agency:") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = car_lb_per_mile, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = car_real_lb_per_mile, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(data = winners_plot, shape = 21, fill = GTA_PURPLE, color = "white", stroke = 1.2, size = 5.5) +
  geom_label_repel(
    data = winners_plot, aes(label = label),
    color = GTA_PURPLE, size = 3.8, nudge_y = 0.38, min.segment.length = 0,
    fill = "white", label.size = 0.2
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = car_lb_per_mile, y = 0.45, hjust = 1.05, size = 3.6,
    label = paste0("Driving alone, CAFE car: ", fmt_2(car_lb_per_mile))
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = car_real_lb_per_mile, y = 0.45, hjust = -0.05, size = 3.6,
    label = paste0("Real-world new car: ", fmt_2(car_real_lb_per_mile))
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.01), breaks = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10)) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.75, 0.9))) +
  labs(
    title = "GTA Greenest Transit Agency awards, 2025",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Pounds of CO2 per passenger-mile (log scale). Large purple labeled ",
      "points = award winners."
    ),
    x = "Pounds of CO2 per passenger-mile (log scale)", y = "Agency size",
    caption = paste0(
      "Sources: FTA National Transit Database 2025 (Energy Consumption; ",
      "Service by Agency); EIA State Electricity Profiles and CO2 ",
      "coefficients;\nNHTSA CAFE MY2026 (~49 mpg); EPA Automotive Trends ",
      "Report (27.2 mpg real-world, MY2024).\nSize by annual trips: Small < ",
      "1M, Medium 1M\u201320M, Large \u2265 20M. Fixed-route agencies with ",
      "\u2265 100K trips; NTD-flagged records excluded."
    )
  ) +
  theme_gta()











Most Emissions Avoided



Hampton Jitney. Photo: Quintin Soloviev, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons


This award measures the total metric tons of CO2 kept out of the atmosphere compared to a scenario where every rider drove alone in a highly efficient CAFE standard car. The Large category winner is MTA New York City Transit (shoutout New York City). They avoided 869,174 metric tons of CO2, which equals taking about 188,951 cars off the road for a year. This is especially impressive since the median large agency actually added 26,068 tons of emissions compared to driving. The Medium winner is Caltrain with 14,909 tons avoided, and the Small winner is Hampton Jitney, Inc. with 5,767 tons avoided.

Battery-Bus Pioneer



Anaheim Regional Transportation (ART) battery-electric bus. Photo: mliu92, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons


This is a custom award for the agency with the highest percentage of its bus energy coming from batteries. Anaheim Regional Transportation in CA wins this year by getting 78% of its bus energy from batteries. For context, across 214 bus fleets with over a million trips, the median battery energy share is 0% (so basically zero). Honorable mentions go to the runners up: Antelope Valley Transit Authority (75%), Link Transit (20%), Mountain Line (17%) (at least they are trying).

NY Waterway ferry. Photo: Beyond My Ken, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons







Glendale Beeline bus. Photo: Evan0512, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons





This is our dishonorable mention for agencies so inefficient that their riders would generate fewer emissions by simply driving alone in a CAFE standard car. We only looked at medium and large agencies with over a million annual trips (so no punching down on the small fleets). The overall worst performer was NY Waterway in NJ. They generate 3.16 lbs of CO2 per passenger-mile, making them 8.3× worse than a solo driver. Since ferries naturally use a lot of energy (but again, they are a vibe sometimes), we also picked a non-ferry winner. Beeline Bus/Dial-A-Ride in CA took that spot by being 8.0× worse than a solo driver. The median medium or large agency is 2.4× worse than a solo driver, showing just how far behind these two agencies really are.
